transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I’m here because I’ve been having trouble with my eating, mostly with certain comfort foods. Once I start, it’s like I keep telling myself, “Maria, that is enough now,” but then my hand just goes back to the pot again anyway. I know I should stop, I really do, and I’m thinking it right there in the moment, but it feels like I can’t quite make myself stop. It’s upsetting, and I guess I finally thought I should talk to someone about it.
How often do these episodes of eating more than you intended happen?

It’s been happening most weeks, I’d say. Not every single day or anything like that, but usually once or twice in a week. It got more noticeable after my friend passed away… those quiet afternoons are the hardest, especially after I come home from choir or from working in the garden. I’ll be by myself, and that’s when it tends to happen.
How do you feel about yourself after one of these eating episodes?

Afterward, I just feel awful about myself, honestly. I feel ashamed… and sad, too. It’s not only that I ate too much, it’s what it means to me, I suppose. Some of those foods used to feel like family, like caring for people, bringing a dish to church or making something the way my mother did. And now, when it happens like that, it feels like I’ve turned it into something secret and ugly, something I’m hiding from people at church.

I’ll sit there afterward and think, “What is wrong with me, Maria?” And then I feel embarrassed, like if anyone knew, they’d look at me differently. It makes me feel very low.
Do you feel like you're eating too much because you can't control your eating, or is it more that you're eating to cope with your emotions?

I think… I think it’s both in a way, but the part that scares me most is the not being able to stop. That’s what brings me here, really. Once I start with those comfort foods, I can be standing right there and saying to myself, Maria, that is enough now. You don’t need any more. And I mean it when I say it. It’s not like I don’t know.

But then my hand goes back to the pot, or I take another bite, and another, and it feels like I can’t quite make myself stop even though I’m telling myself to. It’s like there’s this little argument going on inside me, and the sensible part of me is losing. So yes, I may be upset or lonely, but in the moment it’s that loss of control that really frightens me.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about food or planning when you will eat?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m planning it, no. I don’t sit down in the morning and think, “At three o’clock I’m going to eat this or that.” It doesn’t feel that organized, if that makes sense.

I do think about food in a regular way, you know, like what I need from the store or what I might make, because I’ve always cooked, and cooking has been part of my life for so long. But I don’t know that I spend a lot of time planning when I’ll eat. It’s more that food is just… around in my mind because it’s familiar. I notice it more when I’m alone, maybe, but I wouldn’t say I’m making plans for it ahead of time.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

I’m not really sure, Doctor. I mean, I don’t weigh myself very often—honestly, I tend to avoid it because it makes me nervous and then I start thinking about it too much. My clothes maybe feel a little different some days, but I can’t say if that’s my weight changing or just, you know, how clothes fit depending on the day.

So I don’t think I’ve noticed anything I’d call significant, but I wouldn’t want to say for certain without checking. I just haven’t been keeping track of it closely.
Do you usually feel guilty after eating, even when it's not one of those episodes where you feel like you can't stop?

I don’t know that I usually feel guilty every time, no. I mean, if it’s just a normal meal, like I make myself some toast or have supper, I don’t sit there afterward thinking I’ve done something terrible. At least not most of the time.

Sometimes I might feel a little bothered if I think I ate more than I meant to, even if it wasn’t one of those times where I truly couldn’t stop. But guilt… I’m not sure I’d call it that every time. It’s more like second-guessing myself, maybe. I’ll think, “Did I really need that?” or “Why did I have another serving?” But then other times I just eat and go on with the rest of the evening.

So I guess the answer is, not usually, not after ordinary eating. It’s more confusing than that.
Do you often criticize yourself or feel like you're not good enough in areas of your life unrelated to eating?

I’m not sure I’d say that happens often, no. I mean, I suppose everybody criticizes themselves a little bit, don’t they? Especially when you get older and you look back on things, you can think, “Well, I could’ve done that better,” or “Maybe I should’ve handled that differently.” I do that sometimes.

But feeling like I’m not good enough in general… I don’t know. That’s a hard one to answer. I’m not someone who goes around thinking highly of myself, but I also don’t think I spend all day tearing myself down about everything. If I forget something or don’t get something done the way I wanted, I might get annoyed with myself, but it usually passes.

So I guess I’d say not especially, or at least I haven’t noticed it as a big pattern outside of the eating stuff. It’s more just ordinary second-guessing, I think.
Do you often worry about your weight or body shape?

I’m not really sure I’d say I often worry about it. I mean, I’m aware of it, if that makes sense. At my age, your body isn’t the same as it used to be, and some days I’ll notice how something fits or I’ll catch sight of myself and think, “Well, I don’t like that very much.” But I don’t know that I sit around worrying about my shape all the time.

I do tend to avoid thinking too hard about my weight, honestly. Like I said, weighing myself makes me uneasy, so I don’t do it much. But that’s maybe more because I don’t want to get started down that road of thinking about numbers and whether it’s good or bad. It can make me uncomfortable.

So… I guess I’d put it more as I get bothered by it sometimes, or I’d rather not focus on it, but I don’t know if I’d call it a constant worry. It comes and goes.
Has your eating behavior caused any problems in your relationships or daily activities?

It hasn’t stopped me from doing the main things, no. I still go to Mass, and I still go to choir, and I keep up with my house well enough. I mean, maybe not perfectly, but I do the dishes and the laundry and the ordinary things that need doing.

But after one of those afternoons, when I’ve eaten more than I meant to and I feel embarrassed about it, I do sometimes sort of shut myself in. I’ll think, “Well, I’m not calling anybody now,” or if someone comes to mind that I should check on, I’ll put it off. Not because I don’t care, but because I don’t want to talk and sound normal when I’m feeling that way. I might stay home the rest of the day and just keep to myself.

So I wouldn’t say it’s ruined my relationships or anything like that, but it does make me withdraw a bit afterward. I get ashamed, I guess, and I don’t want anyone noticing.
Do you spend a lot of time thinking about what you've eaten after one of these episodes?

Yes… I suppose I do, though maybe not in a counting-it-all-up sort of way. It’s more that afterward I keep going back over it in my mind, like, “Why did I do that?” or “Why couldn’t I just stop?” And then I feel ashamed.

It makes me sad too, because food always used to mean something good to me, you know? Family, taking care of people, holidays, church suppers, bringing something over when someone was sick. It was a way of showing love, really. And then when I have one of those episodes, it feels like I’ve turned that into something secret and ugly, something I have to hide. Especially from people at church. I wouldn’t want them knowing that side of me.

So yes, I do think about it afterward. Not always every minute, but it sits with me. I feel embarrassed and low, and I keep it to myself.
Have you ever done anything to try to make up for eating too much, like exercising more or skipping meals the next day?

I’m not sure I’d say I do anything deliberate like that. I don’t go out and exercise extra, no. At my age, I’m not the sort to suddenly take a long walk just because I ate too much. And I don’t really think in those terms, like “I have to burn this off” or anything.

Skipping meals… I don’t know. Sometimes the next morning I might not feel very hungry, or I might just have coffee or something small, but I don’t know that it’s me trying to make up for it exactly. It’s more that I feel a bit put off by the whole thing and don’t want to think about food right away. But I’m not planning it out like punishment, if that makes sense.

Mostly I just feel bad about it afterward and try to get back to my usual routine. I don’t have some special thing I do to undo it.
Do you spend more than an hour a day thinking about food or planning meals?

More than an hour a day… I don’t think so, no. I mean, I do think about food in an ordinary way, like what I’m going to have for supper, or if I need to use something before it spoils, or if there’s something at church where I might bring a dish. That’s always been part of my day, really, especially living alone and having to plan for myself.

But if you mean sitting there for hours planning meals or going over food in my head all day, I don’t think it’s like that. Some days I barely plan at all and just have whatever is easy. Other days I might think ahead a bit, especially if I’m going to the store, but I wouldn’t say it takes up that much time most days. It’s not like I’m writing menus or anything.
How often do you find yourself criticizing yourself for things unrelated to eating?

Hmm… unrelated to eating. I’m not sure I’ve really kept track of that. I suppose I do criticize myself sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s more than other people do.

I might get after myself for forgetting something, or not getting around to a chore, or saying something awkward and then thinking about it later. Little things like that. I’ll think, “Well, that was foolish,” or “Why didn’t you handle that better?” But I can’t say how often exactly.

It’s not something I’ve sat down and measured, you know. Some days I’m harder on myself than others. I think I’ve always had a bit of that in me, wanting to do things properly and not be a bother to anyone. But I don’t know that I could give you a number.
Have you ever had a period where you lost a significant amount of weight, only to gain it back?

I don’t think so… not what I would call significant, anyway. My weight has gone up and down some over the years, like I think a lot of people’s does, especially depending on what’s going on in life or how active I am, but I can’t think of a time where I lost a whole lot and then gained it all back.

There have been times I might notice my clothes fitting a little looser, or a little tighter, and then it shifts again, but I haven’t been on some big diet where I dropped a large amount and then put it back on. At least not that I remember. I suppose if you asked me for exact numbers, I wouldn’t be able to tell you very well, because I don’t keep close track like that anymore. But no, nothing that stands out to me as a big weight loss and regain.
How much distress do you feel about your eating behavior in general?

I do feel distressed about it, yes… maybe more than I like to admit. It’s not just, “Oh, I ate too much,” the way people say after a holiday meal. It’s more the feeling afterward that gets to me.

I feel ashamed, mostly. Sad too. Food used to feel like something good to me, you know, something tied up with family and taking care of people — making a casserole, bringing something to church, setting a table. It was about comfort and company. And now sometimes it feels like I’ve turned that into something secretive, something I’m embarrassed about and don’t want anyone at church or anyone who knows me to see.

That’s the part that bothers me. I can act normal enough afterward, I suppose, and I don’t go around telling people, but inside I’ll feel like I’ve done something wrong or let myself down. It leaves me feeling low and sort of… hidden, I guess. Like this thing that ought to be ordinary and caring has become something I keep to myself.
Have you gained a significant amount of weight since these episodes of eating more than you intended started?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I mean, I know my weight isn’t exactly what it was when I was younger — but at 78, I don’t know how much of that is just getting older and being less active and all of that.

Since the eating episodes started… I haven’t kept careful track. I don’t weigh myself regularly, and I think sometimes I avoid it because I don’t especially want to know. My clothes may feel different here and there, but I couldn’t say there’s been some clear, big gain that I can point to and say, “Yes, that happened because of this.”

So… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed a significant amount in any definite way.
How often do you criticize yourself for things you've done or said?

I do that pretty often, I’m afraid. Maybe not every minute of the day, but when I’ve done something I feel bad about, especially with my eating, I can really turn it over and over in my mind.

Afterward I’ll think, “Why did I do that?” or “What’s wrong with me?” And then I feel ashamed and sad. It’s hard to explain, but food used to mean family to me, and caring for people — cooking for others, sharing something, bringing food to church, that kind of thing. And when I eat in a way I don’t feel good about, it feels like I’ve taken something that used to be warm and good and made it into something secretive.

I don’t usually say those things out loud to anyone. I just kind of carry it around inside. I’ll think about how I wouldn’t want people at church to know, and then I criticize myself for hiding it too. So yes… I suppose I do criticize myself quite a bit afterward.
Has your eating behavior affected your ability to participate in activities you enjoy or spend time with friends and family?

Well… yes and no, I suppose. I mean, I still do the things that matter to me. I still go to Mass, and I’m still in choir, and I do take care of my home. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve stopped living my life or anything like that, because I haven’t.

But after one of those afternoons where I’ve eaten more than I meant to, I’m not very eager to be around people. I might stay in the rest of the day, even if I had thought about calling someone or stopping by somewhere. I’ll look at the phone and think about calling a friend or someone from church, and then I just… don’t. I feel embarrassed, even though they wouldn’t necessarily know anything happened.

It’s more that I don’t feel like myself afterward. I feel like I want to keep to myself until that feeling passes. So it hasn’t taken Mass or choir away from me, exactly, but it does make me pull back sometimes, especially right after.
Do you feel like you're unable to control what or how much you're eating during these episodes?

Yes… that’s really the part that scares me, I think. It’s not just that I eat something I enjoy. It’s that once I start, especially with those comfort foods, I’ll tell myself, Maria, that’s enough now. You’ve had enough. And I mean it when I say it to myself.

But then my hand goes right back to the pot, or back for another serving, almost like the thinking part of me and the doing part of me aren’t listening to each other. I’ll be standing there knowing I don’t want to keep eating, and still I do it. That’s what makes me feel so ashamed afterward, because it feels like I should be able to stop if I truly wanted to, but in that moment I just… don’t seem to be able to make myself stop.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about self-criticism for things unrelated to eating, but the symptom profile only covers shame, sadness, or guilt after binge-eating episodes, not general self-criticism outside eating.

patient.answer:
Hmm… unrelated to eating. I’m not sure I’ve really kept track of that. I suppose I do criticize myself sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s more than other people do.

I might get after myself for forgetting something, or not getting around to a chore, or saying something awkward and then thinking about it later. Little things like that. I’ll think, “Well, that was foolish,” or “Why didn’t you handle that better?” But I can’t say how often exactly.

It’s not something I’ve sat down and measured, you know. Some days I’m harder on myself than others. I think I’ve always had a bit of that in me, wanting to do things properly and not be a bother to anyone. But I don’t know that I could give you a number.

doctor.intent: determine presence of significant weight fluctuations
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period where you lost a significant amount of weight, only to gain it back?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of significant weight loss followed by regain, but the provided symptom profile does not include weight cycling or weight change history.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not what I would call significant, anyway. My weight has gone up and down some over the years, like I think a lot of people’s does, especially depending on what’s going on in life or how active I am, but I can’t think of a time where I lost a whole lot and then gained it all back.

There have been times I might notice my clothes fitting a little looser, or a little tighter, and then it shifts again, but I haven’t been on some big diet where I dropped a large amount and then put it back on. At least not that I remember. I suppose if you asked me for exact numbers, I wouldn’t be able to tell you very well, because I don’t keep close track like that anymore. But no, nothing that stands out to me as a big weight loss and regain.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is associated with a significant amount of distress
doctor.question: How much distress do you feel about your eating behavior in general?

target_item.name: Negative_Affect_After_Binge
target_item.manifestation: Afterward I feel ashamed and sad, like I turned something that used to mean family and caring into something I have to hide from people at church.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about distress related to the eating behavior, which is most directly reflected by feeling ashamed, sad, disgusted, depressed, or guilty after binge episodes.

patient.answer:
I do feel distressed about it, yes… maybe more than I like to admit. It’s not just, “Oh, I ate too much,” the way people say after a holiday meal. It’s more the feeling afterward that gets to me.

I feel ashamed, mostly. Sad too. Food used to feel like something good to me, you know, something tied up with family and taking care of people — making a casserole, bringing something to church, setting a table. It was about comfort and company. And now sometimes it feels like I’ve turned that into something secretive, something I’m embarrassed about and don’t want anyone at church or anyone who knows me to see.

That’s the part that bothers me. I can act normal enough afterward, I suppose, and I don’t go around telling people, but inside I’ll feel like I’ve done something wrong or let myself down. It leaves me feeling low and sort of… hidden, I guess. Like this thing that ought to be ordinary and caring has become something I keep to myself.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is associated with a significant amount of weight gain
doctor.question: Have you gained a significant amount of weight since these episodes of eating more than you intended started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant weight gain since the binge-eating episodes began, but the symptom profile provided does not include weight gain or weight change as an item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure, to be honest. I mean, I know my weight isn’t exactly what it was when I was younger — but at 78, I don’t know how much of that is just getting older and being less active and all of that.

Since the eating episodes started… I haven’t kept careful track. I don’t weigh myself regularly, and I think sometimes I avoid it because I don’t especially want to know. My clothes may feel different here and there, but I couldn’t say there’s been some clear, big gain that I can point to and say, “Yes, that happened because of this.”

So… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed a significant amount in any definite way.

doctor.intent: determine frequency of self-criticism
doctor.question: How often do you criticize yourself for things you've done or said?

target_item.name: Negative_Affect_After_Binge
target_item.manifestation: Afterward I feel ashamed and sad, like I turned something that used to mean family and caring into something I have to hide from people at church.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about self-criticism and guilt, which most directly matches feeling ashamed, sad, or guilty after binge-eating episodes.

patient.answer:
I do that pretty often, I’m afraid. Maybe not every minute of the day, but when I’ve done something I feel bad about, especially with my eating, I can really turn it over and over in my mind.

Afterward I’ll think, “Why did I do that?” or “What’s wrong with me?” And then I feel ashamed and sad. It’s hard to explain, but food used to mean family to me, and caring for people — cooking for others, sharing something, bringing food to church, that kind of thing. And when I eat in a way I don’t feel good about, it feels like I’ve taken something that used to be warm and good and made it into something secretive.

I don’t usually say those things out loud to anyone. I just kind of carry it around inside. I’ll think about how I wouldn’t want people at church to know, and then I criticize myself for hiding it too. So yes… I suppose I do criticize myself quite a bit afterward.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Has your eating behavior affected your ability to participate in activities you enjoy or spend time with friends and family?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still go to Mass, choir, and take care of my home, but after one of these afternoons I may stay in and avoid calling anyone because I feel embarrassed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the eating behavior has affected participation in enjoyable activities or time with friends and family, which is most directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well… yes and no, I suppose. I mean, I still do the things that matter to me. I still go to Mass, and I’m still in choir, and I do take care of my home. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve stopped living my life or anything like that, because I haven’t.

But after one of those afternoons where I’ve eaten more than I meant to, I’m not very eager to be around people. I might stay in the rest of the day, even if I had thought about calling someone or stopping by somewhere. I’ll look at the phone and think about calling a friend or someone from church, and then I just… don’t. I feel embarrassed, even though they wouldn’t necessarily know anything happened.

It’s more that I don’t feel like myself afterward. I feel like I want to keep to myself until that feeling passes. So it hasn’t taken Mass or choir away from me, exactly, but it does make me pull back sometimes, especially right after.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's eating behavior is characterized by a lack of control
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to control what or how much you're eating during these episodes?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that once I start eating those comfort foods, I tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough,' but my hand still goes back to the pot like I can’t make myself stop.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether I feel unable to control what or how much I am eating during the episodes.

patient.answer:
Yes… that’s really the part that scares me, I think. It’s not just that I eat something I enjoy. It’s that once I start, especially with those comfort foods, I’ll tell myself, Maria, that’s enough now. You’ve had enough. And I mean it when I say it to myself.

But then my hand goes right back to the pot, or back for another serving, almost like the thinking part of me and the doing part of me aren’t listening to each other. I’ll be standing there knowing I don’t want to keep eating, and still I do it. That’s what makes me feel so ashamed afterward, because it feels like I should be able to stop if I truly wanted to, but in that moment I just… don’t seem to be able to make myself stop.
